newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian separatists seize Venice belltower.
newsitem.headline: Italian separatists seize Venice belltower.

text.p: Up to 10 men, believed by police to be armed, smashed their way into the belltower in St Mark's Square in Venice in a bizarre commando raid on Friday and called for a separate state in northeast Italy.

State radio said the group, dressed in military-style fatigues, had used what appeared to be a six-wheeled armoured vehicle to crash through the entrance to the 99-metre (325-foot) tower after hijacking a public ferry to reach the square.

They hoisted a banner bearing the symbol of the Lion of St Mark from the top of the tower by the Grand Canal and issued a statement describing themselves a regular unit of the "army" of the "Most Serene Republic of Venice".
Around 300 armed police sealed off the world famous square, the lagoon city's biggest tourist draw. Asked whether the group was armed, a police spokesman said: "We think so, we presume they are."
"At this moment the situation is under the control of the forces of order," deputy interior minister Nicola Sinisi said.

It was not immediately clear how police planned to remove the group. One of its members, a young man with his face masked, briefly emerged from the tower and told police: "Don't joke with us. Don't threaten us because we aren't joking either."
The group's secessionist statement was made available to Italian state radio and could also be heard faintly in Venice in a pirate broadcast, apparently from the tower itself.

"After 200 years, a regular unit of the Most Serene Venetian Army has tonight liberated St Mark's Square," the statement said. "The Most Serene Republic of Venice has been reborn today...Long live St Mark."

Venice was for centuries a powerful independent power with territories stretching down the Adriatic and into the Middle East. Known as the "Most Serene Republic" it came to an end on May 12, 1797 when French Napoleonic forces entered the city.

Friday's statement linked the men in the tower to a shadowy group that has been interrupting television news bulletins in the northeast Veneto region for two months with calls for a separate Venetian state.
The pirate broadcasts have spoken of a "spectacular action" in the canal city to mark next Monday's 200th anniversary of the fall of the Venice Republic.

Italian media said the group had forced the captain of a ferry they had boarded shortly after midnight to dock by the square, onto which they drove their military-style vehicle and a minibus and headed for the base of the belltower.

"We knew something might happen around the anniversary of the fall of the Venice republic but no one could have imagined it would come to this," local councillor Mara Rumiz was quoted by the news agency ANSA as saying.
Separatist sentiment has grown in affluent northern Italy in the 1990s, spurred first by political corruption scandals and later by resentment at high taxes and central bureaucacy.

The main secessionist party, the Northern League, last September symbolically declared a separate northern republic of "Padania" at a rally in Venice but has denied it is behind the recent spate of pirate television broadcasts.
"I don't have the slightest idea what is going on," Giancarlo Pagliarini, a member of the League's secessionist "shadow government", said of the Venice belltower assault.
